claim: Neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles (SVs) mediate synaptic transmission.
source: Neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles (SVs) mediate synaptic transmission and are a hallmark specialization in neuronal axons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of synaptic vesicles in neurons.

claim: The leading model for SV protein sorting posits that these proteins are randomly trafficked throughout neurons and are selectively retained in presynaptic boutons.
source: The leading model posits that these proteins are randomly trafficked throughout neurons and are selectively retained in presynaptic boutons.
evidence: This statement references existing models in the field without providing direct citations in this sentence, representing established understanding in the literature.

claim: SYT1 and SYB2 selectively and specifically entered axons with minimal entry into dendrites when expressed at low levels.
source: In sharp contrast to the selective retention model, both proteins selectively and specifically entered axons with minimal entry into dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments.

claim: Moderate overexpression of SV proteins resulted in spillover into dendrites.
source: However, even moderate overexpression resulted in the spillover of SV proteins into dendrites, potentially explaining the origin of previous non-polarized transport models, revealing the limited, saturable nature of the direct axonal trafficking pathway.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data comparing different expression levels.

claim: SV constituents were first delivered to the presynaptic plasma membrane before incorporation into SVs.
source: Moreover, we observed that SV constituents were first delivered to the presynaptic plasma membrane before incorporation into SVs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by pulse-chase experiments using HaloTag labeling.

claim: Axons in a blue whale can reach a length of 30 meters.
source: These highly specialized and asymmetric cells form elaborate axonal and dendritic arbors, with some axons extending great distances (e.g., axons in a blue whale can reach a length of 30 meters; Smith, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith, 2009.

claim: Defects in axonal transport have been implicated in a variety of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Indeed, defects in axonal transport have been implicated in a variety of neurodegenerative diseases (Hung and Link, 2011; Maday et al., 2014; May-simera and Liu, 2013; Vicario-Orri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Anterograde axonal transport of SV proteins is driven by kinesin motors KIF1A and KIF5B.
source: In the case of the axonal transport of SV proteins, anterograde movement is driven by the kinesin motors, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995) and KIF5B (Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003; Song et al., 2009), and retrograde transport is mediated by dynein (Fejtova et al., 2009; Paschal and Vallee, 1987; Schnapp and Reese, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Retrograde transport of SV proteins is mediated by dynein.
source: In the case of the axonal transport of SV proteins, anterograde movement is driven by the kinesin motors, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995) and KIF5B (Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003; Song et al., 2009), and retrograde transport is mediated by dynein (Fejtova et al., 2009; Paschal and Vallee, 1987; Schnapp and Reese, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A direct pathway for dendritic protein sorting is established early in neuronal development.
source: A direct pathway, with proteins traveling directly from the soma to dendrites, is thought to be established early in neuronal development (Burack et al., 2000; Karasmanis et al., 2018; Petersen et al., 2014; Silverman et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The selective retention model proposes non-polarized delivery of axon-destined cargo to both axons and dendrites.
source: The first pathway, often called the selective retention model, is based on the non-polarized delivery of axon-destined cargo to both axons and dendrites. In this pathway, SV proteins that were delivered to axons are retained there, whereas SV proteins that were delivered to the plasma membrane (PM) of dendrites are endocytosed and re-routed back to axons (Fletcher-Jones et al., 2019; Sampo et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes an existing model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The widespread conclusion is that SV proteins are trafficked with a low degree of selectivity into both axons and dendrites of mammalian neurons.
source: After decades of research, the widespread conclusion is that SV proteins are trafficked with a low degree of selectivity into both axons and dendrites of mammalian neurons, and are either selectively retained in, or have partially biased transport toward, axons (Bentley and Banker, 2016).
evidence: This describes the prevailing view in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Recent studies suggest the existence of a direct and selective transport pathway of SV proteins to axons in C. elegans DA9 bipolar neurons and rat and mouse pseudounipolar dorsal root ganglion cells.
source: In contrast to these low-selectivity transport models, recent studies suggest the existence of a direct and selective transport pathway of SV proteins to axons in Caenorhabditis elegans DA9 bipolar neurons and rat and mouse pseudounipolar dorsal root ganglion cells (Gumy et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: VSV-G tsO45 underwent directed polarized axonal transport in mouse hippocampal neurons.
source: One elegant study, using mouse hippocampal neurons, concluded that temperature-sensitive vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV-G tsO45) underwent directed polarized axonal transport (Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SYT1 is a Ca2+ sensor that regulates rapid neurotransmitter release.
source: We focused on synaptotagmin (SYT) 1, a Ca2+ sensor that regulates rapid neurotransmitter release (Chapman, 2008), and synaptobrevin (SYB) 2, a vesicular (v-) SNARE protein, also known as VAMP2, that assembles into trans-SNARE complexes to catalyze membrane fusion (Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chapman, 2008.

claim: SYB2 is a vesicular SNARE protein that assembles into trans-SNARE complexes to catalyze membrane fusion.
source: We focused on synaptotagmin (SYT) 1, a Ca2+ sensor that regulates rapid neurotransmitter release (Chapman, 2008), and synaptobrevin (SYB) 2, a vesicular (v-) SNARE protein, also known as VAMP2, that assembles into trans-SNARE complexes to catalyze membrane fusion (Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Südhof and Rothman, 2009.

claim: SYT1 is a canonical type I transmembrane protein that is co-translationally inserted into the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: These two SV proteins were also selected because SYT1, a canonical type I transmembrane protein, is co-translationally inserted into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Perin et al., 1990; Shao and Hegde, 2011), whereas SYB2, a type II tail-anchored protein, is post-translationally inserted into the ER (Kutay et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perin et al., 1990 and Shao and Hegde, 2011.

claim: SYB2 is a type II tail-anchored protein that is post-translationally inserted into the ER.
source: These two SV proteins were also selected because SYT1, a canonical type I transmembrane protein, is co-translationally inserted into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Perin et al., 1990; Shao and Hegde, 2011), whereas SYB2, a type II tail-anchored protein, is post-translationally inserted into the ER (Kutay et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kutay et al., 1995.

claim: SYT1 is trafficked by the kinesin motor KIF1A.
source: Moreover, SYT1 and SYB2 have been shown to be trafficked by different kinesin motors, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995) and KIF5B (Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003; Song et al., 2009), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Okada et al., 1995.

claim: SYB2 is trafficked by the kinesin motor KIF5B.
source: Moreover, SYT1 and SYB2 have been shown to be trafficked by different kinesin motors, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995) and KIF5B (Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003; Song et al., 2009), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakata and Hirokawa, 2003 and Song et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpression results in the spillover of SV proteins into inappropriate compartments.
source: In these experiments, careful attention was paid to expression levels since overexpression results in the spillover of SV proteins into inappropriate compartments, thus obscuring polarized transport (Pennuto et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pennuto et al., 2003.

claim: The RUSH system allows proteins of interest to be retained in the ER and released upon addition of biotin.
source: In the RUSH system, proteins of interest are retained in the ER and released upon addition of the small molecule, biotin.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the RUSH system used in the study.

claim: Upon release of ER-tethered SYT1, there was little to no transport activity in proximal dendrites.
source: Upon release of ER-tethered SYT1, we observed little to no transport activity in proximal dendrites (defined as the first 20 µm of the neurite) as shown by the lack of diagonal lines in the kymograph (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis showing minimal movement in dendrites.

claim: There was noticeable movement of tagged SYT1 as it began to egress from the soma directly into axons in an anterograde direction.
source: however, there was noticeable movement of tagged SYT1 as it began to egress from the soma directly into axons in an anterograde direction, as represented in the kymograph by diagonal lines with a negative slope (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis showing anterograde movement in axons.

claim: The majority of anterograde-moving vesicles observed in proximal axons did not contain the co-expressed ER-targeted GFP.
source: We highlight that the majority of anterograde-moving vesicles observed in proximal axons did not contain the co-expressed ER-targeted GFP (Figure 1F), confirming that these are post-ER organelles.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing separation of SYT1 signal from ER marker.

claim: The stationary SYT1 signal in proximal dendrites colocalized with ER-targeted GFP.
source: In contrast, the stationary SYT1 signal in proximal dendrites colocalized with ER-targeted GFP (Figure 1E), indicating the observed signal is protein in the ER, rather than post-Golgi transport vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis of SYT1 with ER marker in dendrites.

claim: Robust transport of the SYT1 reporter was observed in proximal and distal axons.
source: As was first seen in Figure 1, we again observed robust transport of the SYT1 reporter in proximal axons and extended these observations to distal axons
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis in multiple axonal regions.

claim: Proximal and distal dendrites had little to no detectable trafficking of SYT1-containing transport vesicles.
source: proximal and distal dendrites had little to no detectable trafficking of SYT1-containing transport vesicles (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis showing minimal transport in dendrites.

claim: The SYB2 reporter showed the same trafficking pattern as SYT1, with transport primarily in axons and minimal transport in dendrites.
source: This trend was also observed for the SYB2 reporter, allowing us to generalize our findings to topologically distinct SV proteins that are transported by different kinesin motors (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis of SYB2 transport.

claim: Both SYT1 and SYB2 reporters were preferentially transported in the anterograde direction in axons.
source: Of the transport vesicles observed, both SYT1 and SYB2 reporters were preferentially transported in the anterograde direction in axons (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of vesicle displacement showing anterograde bias.

claim: SYB2 was transported more slowly in the proximal axon compared to the distal axon.
source: We note that SYB2 was transported more slowly in the proximal axon, which encompasses the AIS, as compared to the distal axon; SYT1 transport did not slow down in the AIS (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Song et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of transport speeds in different axonal regions.

claim: TfR was overwhelmingly trafficked to dendrites without passing through axons.
source: Using the same criteria as Figure 2 to select proximal and distal regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), we observed that TfR was overwhelmingly trafficked to dendrites without passing through axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–F), even when purposefully overexpressed.
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis showing dendritic transport of TfR.

claim: When SYT1 was drastically overexpressed via transfection, it spilled over into dendrites and coated the PM of all neurites.
source: Indeed, in agreement with previous studies, when we drastically overexpressed SYT1 via transfection, it spilled over into dendrites and "coated" the PM of all neurites; it also caused the growth of filopodia-like structures in the somatodendritic domain (Figure 3A; Feany et al., 1993b).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing mislocalization at high expression levels.

claim: At low expression levels, the SYT1 and SYB2 reporters showed polarized, presynaptic distribution characteristic of SV proteins.
source: Only when expression levels were low—effectively indistinguishable from the endogenous protein—and the dimmest cells were selected, did we observe the polarized, presynaptic distribution of the SYT1 and SYB2 reporters, at steady state, that is characteristic of SV proteins (Figure 3F and G; Chapman, 2008; Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data at different expression levels and citations to established SV protein characteristics.

claim: The low, intermediate, and high expression levels resulted in 1.14-, 1.22-, and 2.48-fold increases over the wild type SYT1 levels at the synapse, respectively.
source: This analysis revealed that the low, intermediate, and high expression levels resulted in 1.14-, 1.22-, and 2.48-fold increases over the wild type (WT) SYT1 levels at the synapse, respectively, and 0.93-, 1.17-, and 1.87-fold changes for SYB2 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative ICC analysis comparing fluorescence intensities.

claim: The low, intermediate, and high expression levels resulted in 0.93-, 1.17-, and 1.87-fold changes for SYB2 at the synapse.
source: This analysis revealed that the low, intermediate, and high expression levels resulted in 1.14-, 1.22-, and 2.48-fold increases over the wild type (WT) SYT1 levels at the synapse, respectively, and 0.93-, 1.17-, and 1.87-fold changes for SYB2 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative ICC analysis comparing fluorescence intensities.

claim: At high expression levels, both the SYT1 and SYB2 reporters appeared throughout the PM of cells and spilled over into internal structures in dendrites.
source: In addition to the relatively modest overexpression observed at individual synapses, both the SYT1 and SYB2 reporters also appeared throughout the PM of cells and spilled over into internal structures in dendrites at high expression levels (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing mislocalization at high expression.

claim: SYT1 is both palmitoylated and glycosylated.
source: Although sorting motifs are not yet defined for this protein, it is both palmitoylated (Chapman et al., 1996; Heindel et al., 2003) and glycosylated (Perin et al., 1991), and both modifications have been proposed to play roles in its trafficking (Kang et al., 2004; Han et al., 2004; Atiya-Nasagi et al., 2005; but see also Kwon and Chapman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Palmitoylation and glycosylation of SYT1 have been proposed to play roles in its trafficking.
source: Although sorting motifs are not yet defined for this protein, it is both palmitoylated (Chapman et al., 1996; Heindel et al., 2003) and glycosylated (Perin et al., 1991), and both modifications have been proposed to play roles in its trafficking (Kang et al., 2004; Han et al., 2004; Atiya-Nasagi et al., 2005; but see also Kwon and Chapman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies, with a note of conflicting evidence.

claim: The full-length SYT1 reporter was correctly targeted to synapses, as confirmed by its colocalization with synaptophysin.
source: The full-length SYT1 reporter was included as a positive control and was correctly targeted to synapses, as confirmed by its colocalization with the synaptic marker, synaptophysin (SYP) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis with a synaptic marker.

claim: The SYT1-PGM construct accumulated in the soma as well as the axonal compartment, where it was colocalized with SYP.
source: The SYT1-PGM construct accumulated in the soma as well as the axonal compartment, where it was colocalized with SYP; it was virtually undetectable in dendrites, similar to our findings using the WT SYT1 reporter (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and colocalization analysis.

claim: The truncated SYT1 protein, SYT1ΔC2AB, was present throughout axons and was also observed in the somatodendritic compartment, indicating mistargeting of the protein.
source: The truncated SYT1 protein, SYT1ΔC2AB, was present throughout axons, likely on the PM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Courtney et al., 2019), and was also observed in the somatodendritic compartment, indicating mistargeting of the protein (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing distribution in multiple compartments.

claim: In knockout neurons, the WT SYT1 reporter was trafficked in a polarized manner to axons.
source: In knockout neurons, the WT SYT1 reporter was—again—trafficked in a polarized manner to axons (Figure 4F and I).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis in SYT1 knockout neurons.

claim: SYT1-PGM was selectively trafficked to axons, consistent with observations of the WT protein.
source: In contrast to previous studies (Han et al., 2004; Kang et al., 2004; Atiya-Nasagi et al., 2005), but consistent with our findings under steady state, SYT1-PGM was selectively trafficked to axons, consistent with our observations of the WT protein (Figure 4G and I).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis showing axonal transport of the mutant.

claim: The SYT1ΔC2AB construct entered axons and dendrites at similar rates, with a non-significant trend toward preferential entrance into axons.
source: Conversely, the SYT1ΔC2AB construct entered axons and dendrites at similar rates, with a non-significant trend toward preferential entrance into axons (p=0.49) (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of transport vesicles in different compartments.

claim: The tandem C2-domains of SYT1 play a role in the proper targeting of SYT1.
source: Taken together, these experiments reveal that the tandem C2-domains play a role in the proper targeting of SYT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing mistargeting of the C2AB deletion mutant.

claim: Palmitoylation and glycosylation were dispensable for selective targeting of SYT1 to axons.
source: In contrast, palmitoylation and glycosylation were dispensable for selective targeting of SYT1 to axons.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that the PGM mutant was still selectively trafficked to axons.

claim: It has long been hypothesized that SV proteins are first delivered to the presynaptic PM as the final destination of their maiden voyage to synapses.
source: It has long been hypothesized that SV proteins, prior to their incorporation onto nascent SVs, are first delivered to the presynaptic PM as the final destination of their maiden voyage to synapses (Buckley et al., 2000; Feany and Buckley, 1993a; Hannah et al., 1999; Régnier-Vigouroux et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes a hypothesis in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic activity and SV recycling were inhibited by expression of TeTx-LC, which cleaves endogenous SYB2.
source: To minimize this potential confound, the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeTx-LC) was co-expressed, using lentivirus, to cleave endogenous SYB2 and inhibit synaptic activity and SV recycling (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Bao et al., 2018; Schiavo et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data and electrophysiology showing reduced synaptic activity.

claim: In cultures grown in the absence of JF549i, there was a dramatic increase in fluorescence intensity at synapses upon addition of permeant JF549 for both SYT1 and SYB2.
source: As expected, in cultures grown in the absence of JF549i, we observed a dramatic increase in the fluorescence intensity at synapses upon the addition of permeant JF549 for both SYT1 and SYB2.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fluorescence changes in the pulse-chase experiment.

claim: Synapses cultured with JF549i for 6 days exhibited minimal changes in fluorescence after addition of permeant JF549.
source: However, synapses cultured with JF549i for 6 days exhibited minimal changes in fluorescence after addition of permeant JF549.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fluorescence changes in the pulse-chase experiment.

claim: Delivery of SYT1 and SYB2 to the presynaptic PM creates a depot from which SV biogenesis can occur.
source: In light of these findings, we propose that delivery of SYT1 and SYB2 to the presynaptic PM creates a depot from which SV biogenesis can occur.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pulse-chase experiments showing PM delivery.

claim: For the past two decades, the leading model posits that axonal proteins are delivered indiscriminately to all neurites and are subsequently selectively retained in axons.
source: For the past two decades, the leading model posits that axonal proteins are delivered indiscriminately to all neurites and are subsequently selectively retained in axons (Bentley and Banker, 2016; Sampo et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The transport of dendritic cargos has been shown to be selective, with vesicles carrying dendritic cargo trafficked directly to dendrites without entering axons.
source: In sharp contrast, the transport of dendritic cargos has been shown to be selective, and vesicles carrying dendritic cargo are trafficked directly to dendrites without entering axons.
evidence: This describes established findings about dendritic cargo transport.

claim: Without careful control of expression levels, direct transport is obscured by the spillover and mistargeting of cargo into other compartments of neurons.
source: As we show, without the careful control of expression levels, direct transport is obscured by the spillover and mistargeting of cargo into other compartments of neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression level experiments in the study.

claim: SV proteins seem to be particularly susceptible to mistargeting due to overexpression, as intentional overexpression of TfR did not affect its selective transport to dendrites.
source: We note that SV proteins seem to be particularly susceptible to this artifact, as the intentional overexpression of TfR did not appear to affect its selective transport to dendrites.
evidence: This is based on comparison of overexpression effects between SV proteins and TfR.

claim: A rigorous study focusing on nematode DA9 bipolar neurons revealed that SYB2 was delivered directly to presynaptic boutons.
source: Namely, a rigorous study focusing on nematode DA9 bipolar neurons revealed that SYB2 was delivered directly to presynaptic boutons (Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Experiments using dorsal root ganglion cells from mouse and rat suggested MAP2-dependent selective cargo sorting and transport of axonal proteins.
source: Experiments using dorsal root ganglion cells from mouse and rat suggested MAP2-dependent selective cargo sorting and transport of axonal proteins (Gumy et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A more recent study using mouse neurons indicated that axonal proteins do not enter dendrites.
source: A more recent study, using mouse neurons, indicated that axonal proteins do not enter dendrites (Karasmanis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Glycosylation and palmitoylation were dispensable for direct transport of SYT1 to axons.
source: We also used the RUSH assay to conduct structure-function studies of SYT1 and found that glycosylation and palmitoylation were dispensable for direct transport to axons.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that the PGM mutant showed normal axonal transport.

claim: Removing the C2-domains of SYT1 did not affect axonal transport, but increased transport into dendrites, thereby disrupting the polarized distribution of this protein.
source: In contrast, removing the C2-domains of SYT1 did not affect axonal transport, but rather increased transport into dendrites, thereby disrupting the polarized distribution of this protein.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of transport in the C2AB deletion mutant.

claim: The initial fusion reaction of SV proteins at the presynaptic PM is potentially mediated via tetanus-insensitive VAMP, called VAMP7.
source: This initial fusion reaction is potentially mediated via tetanus-insensitive VAMP, called VAMP7 (Galli et al., 1998; Chaineau et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on citations to previous studies about VAMP7.

claim: During normal recycling, SYT1 is internalized via its tandem C2-domains, potentially via mechanisms that mediate SV retrieval from the PM.
source: Then, during normal recycling, SYT1 is internalized via its tandem C2-domains, potentially via mechanisms that mediate SV retrieval from the PM (Courtney et al., 2019; Jarousse et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies about SYT1 internalization.

claim: Efficient retrieval of SYB2 is mediated by its interaction with SYP.
source: and efficient retrieval of SYB2 is mediated by its interaction with SYP (Gordon et al., 2011; Harper et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is no longer thought to mediate the internalization of SV proteins.
source: Retrieval may involve interactions with various adaptor proteins, but the emerging view is that these interactions are unlikely to occur at the PM, as clathrin-mediated endocytosis is no longer thought to mediate the internalization of SV proteins (Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hippocampal neurons were dissected from pre-natal Sprague-Dawley rats on E18.
source: Hippocampal neurons were dissected from pre-natal Sprague-Dawley rats on E18 (Envigo), or post-natal SYT1 conditional knockout floxed mice (Quadros et al., 2017) on P0-P1.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Rat neurons were plated at a density of 125,000 cells per coverslip.
source: Rat neurons were plated on 18 mm coverslips Warner instruments, 64-0734 (CS-18R17) that had been coated with poly-D-lysine (Thermo Fisher Scientific, ICN10269491) for 1 hr at room temperature, at a density of 125,000 cells per coverslip, in supplemented DMEM.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: For RUSH release experiments, neurons were transduced with the streptavidin hook virus on 8 DIV and transduced with a reporter virus on 9 DIV.
source: For RUSH release experiments, neurons were transduced with the streptavidin hook virus on 8 DIV and transduced with a reporter virus on 9 DIV.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline used in the study.

claim: Cells were imaged on 14–16 DIV.
source: Cells were imaged on 14–16 DIV.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline used in the study.

claim: Videos were acquired approximately 20–30 min after biotin addition.
source: Videos were acquired ~20–30 min after biotin addition at 1 frame per second with a Zeiss 880 Airyscan LSM microscope and 63× objective using Fast Airyscan mode.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and timing used in the study.
